1.description:
Climate change here describes the wide range of effects resulting from human-caused disruption to atmospheric and oceanic carbon cycling. The influence of humans on the global climate system is primarily due to the emission of greenhouse gases into the atmosphere. These effects include rapid global heating, alterations to long-term large-scale climatic patterns such as global circulatory systems, altered local weather patterns, shifts in historic climate regions, and the localised biotic and abiotic responses to these changes.

Note on climate change projections

Modelling is used to project the future impacts of climate change, the exact pathways of which are uncertain due to different possible responses to climate change. Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) are used to project a range of climate change scenarios which account for different concentrations of greenhouse gas emissions resulting from different economic, social and physical responses[123]. This factor page primarily notes the two most extreme scenarios:

  • Best case scenario (RCP2.6): This is the most benign scenario in which future emissions are severely restricted to limit future climate change, although significant change is still projected.
  • Worst case scenario (RCP8.5): This is the most extreme scenario which aligns with the current global emission trajectory.

Under any available scenario average global temperatures will increase with far reaching impacts across the planet during the coming years and decades.

3.impact:
Climate change has compound impacts on other factors. These are briefly laid out below with more detail on each of the relevant factor pages.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Due to climate change having unequal impacts globally, as a result of both physical and socio-economic conditions, international migration of people may increase the UK population and/or change the character of the UK population as a whole. Additionally, there may be increased demand for housing in rural areas as a result of disproportionate population growth and warming in urban areas. As a result, the Peak District may experience changes to the demographic character of both its residents and its visitors due to global and local population changes. There is little research into exactly what these changes may look like, however projections do indicate that current migration trends are likely to be amplified as a result of climate change[64].

Ecological change

The projected impacts of climate change are intrinsically linked to potential ecological changes. As the physical conditions which define species’ niches shift, both spatially and temporally, species distribution and phenology (timing of biological events) will change.

Cooke et al. (2026) model biodiversity change in the UK under a range of climate scenarios up to 2080[61]. They project “extensive community reorganisation” under any scenario with “the disappearance of current bioclimates and emergence of novel ones”. In the Peak District, this is likely to contribute to the local extinction of species, colonisation by novel species, changes to composition of biological communities, increase likelihood of invasive alien species and increased likelihood of pathogens.

Formulating and setting habitat and species targets, as has been the practice for many years, will need to be carefully re-examined as an approach.

Land management practices

Climate change is likely to drive significant and rapid change in land management practices as a result of how land managers and society respond to climate change. Projections from the European Environment Agency indicate that agricultural land value is likely to fall by as much as 80% in southern European and rise by up to 60% northern Europe by 2100, while the UK may see a 20% rise, possibly up to 40% in Scotland[62]. This is indicative of the change in agricultural productivity in these areas; in the UK, land value increase could result in increased arable agriculture to replace lost crop land in southern Europe.

Brown et al. (2022) detail how under different climate change and socioeconomic scenarios, different types of land use change may result, however under all scenarios change is projected[63]. This research indicates that while it is difficult to predict the exact change that may occur, changing land management practise are likely in the Peak District, in part as a response to climate change.

Pollution

The understanding of effect of climate change on pollution is beginning to be better understood, with research in to heavy metal pollution, particulates, sewage release and chemical interactions in their infancy. Uncontrolled vegetation fires, so called ‘wildfire’, is however better understood and a present and growing problem. The increased incidence of wildfires that is likely to result from climate change will cause the emission of more airborne particulate pollution as a result of burnt vegetation. Recent vegetation burning demonstrates that airborne particulate pollution travels large distances and has health impacts beyond the boundary of the Peak District[118] as well as direct impacts on ecosystem services and benefits such as water supply.

Visitation and access

Climate change may directly contribute to increased visitor numbers in the Peak District National Park during heatwave events. As extremes of temperature and humidity are projected to be greater in urban areas[52], people may seek cooler outdoor spaces during these events. Additionally, domestic tourism may increase if the popularity of overseas destinations declines due to extreme heat in countries at lower latitudes, an emerging trend observed in recent warmer years. A study of the impact of heat waves on Spanish tourism showed that during heatwaves, UK tourist number significantly declined, which could indicate that these tourists will increasingly seek domestic tourist destinations like the Peak District during these events[60].

Additionally, it is possible that climate change may result in changes to visitor behaviour, such as a longer peak tourist season and changes to visitor hotspots, as visitors seek out respite from extremes of temperature and humidity. Data, and anecdotal reports from European protected areas and popular tourist destinations around the world, including UK protected areas, are showing extended visitor seasons. Consistent reports indicate a change from traditional seasonal peaks to ‘flatter’ year round visitation patterns, an overall increase in visitor days, and the consequent positive and negative impact on the environment, local communities and local economies.

2.description: Demographic and sociocultural change refers to features of human populations, for example the distribution of age, race and employment among people in a place. This also includes change to the ways humans interact and relate to each other through behaviour carried out across populations. This may result in changes to the ways people live and care for each other, what people consume, what people think, and what ideologies are dominant or minoritised. These changes can result from or relate to global change such as climate change, changing trends in technology especially relating to communication, and political changes.

4.impact:
Climate change

As outlined on the Climate change factor page, Representative Concentration Pathway modelling accounts for different future greenhouse gas emissions scenarios that result from different responses to climate change. These responses are profoundly shaped by social trends and demographic characteristics. Therefore, all climate change scenarios are intrinsically linked to demographic and sociocultural changes.

Governance and legislation

Potential changes to governance and legislation that impact the National Park are in turn impacted by social trends. For example, the changes in social attitudes to outdoor recreation discussed above could contribute to changes in access legislation if more people demand and campaign for an increased right to countryside access for recreation.

Land management practices

The Shared Socioeconomic Pathways discussion on the Land management practises factor page exemplify how demographic and sociocultural change could impact land management. Under different socio-economic scenarios, these pathways can be used to describe different possible future land use scenarios in the UK.

Visitation and access

Patterns and trends of visitation and access in the National Park are likely to be impacted by changes in the demographic and sociocultural character of both Peak District resident and visitors. This could result in impacts such as change to visitor numbers and changes in the behaviour of visitors due to changing attitudes to outdoor recreation.

3.description:
Ecological change refers to changes within and between species of plants, animals, fungi and microbes resulting from multiple factors including climate change, changing land management practises, and pollution. This could include changes to an individual species behaviour, life cycle, phenology (biological timings), population size, range and intra-species interactions. Consequently, this also includes changes to the species diversity and abundance of ecosystems, altered habitat types and biomes present in a given area, and changes to interactions between species including predation, herbivory, mutualism and parasitism. Where these changes occur, there will be a shift in the functionality of ecological systems resulting in changes to the ecosystem services they deliver.

Note on projection of future climate and socioeconomic scenarios

Research which models future change to ecological communities needs to account for possible future climate change and socioeconomic scenarios, the exact pathways of which are are uncertain due to different possible global, national and local actions. To do this, models for multiple future climate and socioeconomic pathways are used to project a range of possible future scenarios.

Climate models

Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) are used to project a range of climate change scenarios which account for different concentrations of greenhouse gas emissions[123]. This page primarily notes the two most extreme scenarios:

  • Best case scenario (RCP2.6): Future emissions are severely restricted to limit future climate change, although significant change is still projected.
  • Worst case scenario (RCP8.5): Continued current global emission trajectory.

Socioeconomic models

Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) describe a range of scenarios for societal development[100]. This page also references the two extremes of these scenarios as used in ecological research:

  • Sustainability (SSP1): A political and social shift toward environmentally sustainable technological, economic and energy sectors.
  • Fossil-fuelled development (SSP5): Continued production of and demand for fossil fuels for manufacturing.

5.impact:
Climate change

Change in ecological communities could alter the potential for carbon storage in biomass, which will impact the possibility for land-based mitigation of greenhouse gas emissions as is accounted for in net zero targets. For example, changes to blanket bog communities could result in less accumulation of peat soil, reducing carbon storage potential, and in the possible release of additional carbon from soil due to runoff, resulting in enhanced climate change. Ecological communities may also experience non-linear shifts, for example a sudden collapse in function in single biome, which could in turn provoke non-linear climatic impacts due to the impact on water, carbon and nutrient cycling.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Ecological change could impact on the demography and sociocultural practices of both residents and visitors to the Peak District due to the connections between people and their wider ecologies. Shifts in ecological communities could invoke changes to the composition of rural communities, as the possibility for agricultural livelihoods changes and people’s connection to and sense of belonging in the landscape shifts. Additionally, visitors to the Peak District come in part to interact with the ecology of the landscape, from foraging to taking in the view. Changes to these communities may result in different people visiting in different ways.

Land management practices

Land management practices take place in relation to the underlying ecological communities. Therefore, changes to this ecology are likely to result in changed land management practices. For example, in the Peak District, uplands currently managed for grouse moors may be managed differently if the red grouse experiences population decline and the composition upland moorland habitats shift to make this form of moorland management no longer sustainable. Similarly, agricultural practices may have to change if different compositions of agri-ecological systems emerge, pests and diseases impact on crops and livestock, etc.

Pollution

The potential destabilisation of moorland soils as a result of changes to upland vegetation communities could resulting in the wash out of heavy metal pollution stored in these soils from industrial revolution. This would have downstream consequences as this pollution is spread, potentially having further ecological impacts as well as impacting agricultural land and drinking water.

4.description:
Governance describes systems, processes and mechanisms of taking decisions which inform action taken by organisations, public bodies and other groups, while legislation describes the laws and legal systems to encourage or condemn certain actions. Supporting policy and regulation exist to further clarify, monitor and enforce action. Therefore, governance and legislation result from national, regional, local and organisational decisions regarding which actions are permissible and promoted and which are outlawed.

It is not possible to have much certainty over projections of changes to governance and legislation as this factor is impacted by so many other factors in turn, from popular mood to political power. Therefore, the below projections are sometimes contradictory estimations on possible future changes related to legislation and governance. All carry a relatively low certainty.

6.impact:
Governance and legislation have the potential to impact all other factors due to the legislation and governance frameworks that underlie all action carried out in the UK. This could be drawn together in an almost infinite number of links, however certainty about what impacts are likely is very low, and many relevant ways in which governance and legislation impacts other factors have already been outlined above. Therefore, these are briefly summarised below with some additional impacts that have not yet been noted.

Factor

Possible impacts from governance and legislation

Climate change

Stronger commitments to emissions reduction and carbon sequestration and storage could help to reduce likelihood of global climate change impacts, e.g. changes to the Climate Change Act 2008 or additional global agreements.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Impacts on communities from changes to planning regulation (NFFP, local plan making process etc) could alter housing development in communities, potential knock-on impact to composition of communities.

Ecological change

Possibility for strengthened or weakened environmental protections, e.g. through BNG and biodiversity credits, changes to National Park legislation and governance, etc. Land use framework, LNRSs and 30x30 target may introduce stronger requirements and spatial planning for land to be managed for ecology.

Economy and industry

Changes to farm subsidy schemes may positively or negatively impact he viability of farm businesses. More NSIPs to support low carbon energy and transport infrastructure could support construction and operation jobs.

Land management practices

Farm subsidies and land management grants may incentivise changes to land uses and management actions. Land use framework may change how land use is determined. Changes to land ownership resulting in changed land management may result from enhance community right to buy to England[98].

Possible changes to legislation relating to driven grouse shooting, including further changes to moorland burning regulation about and an ongoing campaign to ban on driven grouse shooting[99], may result to changes in moorland management.

Pollution

Changes to the regulation of sewage waste outflow into freshwater would reduce freshwater pollution. Legislation relating to land management outline above could change agricultural pollution e.g. lower input farming reducing nutrient pollution.

Visitation and access

New access legislation could strength right to access, including permitted activities and areas with open access. Combined authorities may use visitor levies which could impact visitor access by presenting financial barrier, may cause inequality in access.

5.description: Land management practices are the sets of actions undertaken which shape the ways land is used by people. Different practices will be carried out to achieve different outcomes, such as food production, natural resource extraction or biodiversity conservation. Which outcomes are chosen is affected by who owns, occupies or has the right to manage land, the historical ways the land has been used, both the biological and physical conditions of the area (e.g. underlying geology) as well as economic and socio-cultural factors.

7.impact:
Climate change

As described above, land can be managed to mitigate the impacts of climate change by sequestering or preventing the further emission of fossil fuels. If the Peak District was managed to maximise this, it could help remove CO2 from the atmosphere to slow future climate change. However, on the scale of the Peak District this would have a relatively small impact on global climate change.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Where land management and ownership change, this could have consequences for the demographics of rural and farming communities, based on who is able to live and work in the Peak District. If land is consolidated under fewer ownership, this could mean that fewer people live and work on the land. However, changes to farming or conservation land management practices may result in more rural jobs. Therefore, it is difficult to make projections about exactly what these changes may look like.

Pollution

Certain land management practices can either result in or reduce pollution. Fertiliser run off from agricultural land can cause polluting effects in freshwater systems, and therefore moving toward lower input agricultural land management can reduce this pollution. Land management practices which stabilise soils, for example peatland restoration, can result in reduced top soil runoff and therefore less sediment contaminated with pollutants from industrial air pollution ending up downstream.

Visitation and access

The Peak District is widely known among visitors for its landscapes under their current management regimes, which promote people to visit the area and participate in different recreational activities. If land was managed differently, this could change people’s perception of the landscape and alter their visiting behaviour, as well as possible changes to access infrastructure which would need to adapt around changing land use.  This could be in the direction of reduced access and declining visitation, for example under agriculture intensification, or it could be increased visitation through ecotourism.

6.description: Pollution is the harmful release or emission, whether accidental or intentional, of substances or energy into the natural environment which can result in harm to organisms, ecosystems or natural functions. This can include air, water, soil, light and noise pollution.

8.impact:
Climate change

Particulate pollution can contribute towards climate change as a result of airborne particulates absorbing heat and light, contributing to atmospheric warming and cloud formation[118].

Ecological changes

Water pollution alters the chemical environment for aquatic life, impacting species’ abilities to reproduce. Excess nutrients or changes to pH cause imbalance with some species thriving at the expense of others, resulting changes to the diversity and composition of aquatic ecosystems. This can also have knock on impacts on terrestrial ecosystems which interact with polluted water sources[119].

Nitrogen air pollution alters lichen community composition, with some species being nitrogen-tolerant and others nitrogen-sensitive. In this was lichens can be used as indicators of nitrogen air pollution[120].

7.description: Visitation describes the use of the National Park for leisure and recreation, either by residents or tourists travelling into the Peak District. Access refers to the structures which facilitate this such as paths, tracks, trails, tourism infrastructure and interpretation.

9.impact:
Ecological Change

Visitation and access has the potential to affect ecological change if it leads to impacts such as soil compaction and habitat degradation. Roadside verges have been identified as agricultural settings that may be rich in wildflowers and meadow species can be prone to invasion of more dominant ruderal species due to the nature of disturbance and additional nitrogen that occurs alongside roads and higher levels of traffic[71].

Pollution

If there are changes to visitor numbers, the current prevalence of car travel in how people access the National Park could have an effect on pollution: contributing to carbon emissions as well as noise and light pollution. The knock on demand for car or public transport related infrastructure could also therefore generate further embedded carbon and generate emissions during production.
